extracted.intended_audience: writers and teachers of creative writing (workshop leaders, students, emerging writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for instructors and participants on how to use workshop practices and short craft essays (e.g., Glimmer Train Bulletin) to develop writers' skills; focuses on critique-writing, revision, and classroom expectations. Useful for those designing or participating in fiction workshops and classroom assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop is for writing critiques, not receiving them
rubrics_metrics.description: The real learning in workshop often comes from writing critiques, not receiving them. (Quoted: 'Workshop is not for you' — meaning the act of critiquing others develops the writer.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being forced to analyze the effectiveness of other writers’ stories and to then provide them with clear, concise, specific suggestions for improvement will do more to develop a writer’s craft than almost anything else. Through critiquing, writers develop objectivity about their own work, sharpen critical thinking, and hone language. Instructors can use this framing to console students who expect reciprocity and to assign critique-writing as central practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write clear, concise, specific workshop feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Feedback should be clear, concise, and specific, offering concrete suggestions for improvement rather than vague praise or generalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good commentary identifies concrete problems (e.g., flat dialogue, abrupt scenes, uneven pacing) and offers specific recommendations. Students who diligently read peers' work and produce thoughtful feedback gain craft benefits even if they don't receive equal feedback in return. Emphasize actionable items and examples in written comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set and manage workshop expectations / social contract
rubrics_metrics.description: Workshop participants often expect reciprocity (comments on their own work); instructors should clarify that workshop's primary pedagogical value may lie elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the social contract appears broken (students feel cheated by lack of returned feedback), reframe workshop goals toward skill development via critique-writing. Explicitly tell students the purpose (e.g., 'Workshop is not for you') and design assignments that foreground learning by critiquing rather than guaranteeing returned comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision is where writing happens
rubrics_metrics.description: Revision is the central phase in which stories' subtleties and strategies develop; initial drafts are often 'hallucinations' that revision grounds into craft and truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage multiple revision passes as a deliberate craft practice. Emphasize that revision offers the possibility to 'make things right' and to find truth in an idea. Teach revision techniques and foster a mindset that values re-working; contrast the rush of initial inspiration with the sustained work of re-crafting. The author claims: 'Revision separates wannabes from writers.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Embrace rigorous, honest instruction (even if harsh)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tough, honest mentorship—though it may provoke anger—can be formative and lead to significant improvement and publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Share anecdotes that tough critiques can produce durable benefits; normalize the emotional discomfort of candid feedback and encourage students to extract the instructive content. Use instructors' honest, exacting comments as models for high-quality critique and revision prompts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value consistent writing practice; treat writing days as victories
rubrics_metrics.description: Regularly making time to write is itself valuable; even imperfect or discouraging sessions are productive in aggregate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject the notion that writing depends on a separate 'writing self' and instead cultivate habit and discipline. Reinforce that 'The days that I write are victories' and that time spent writing is time well spent; incorporate assignments and accountability to promote consistent practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use short craft essays and resources (e.g., Glimmer Train Bulletin) in teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Micro-essays on craft (such as those in Glimmer Train’s Bulletin) are useful resources for both writers and teachers and can be used in classrooms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Glimmer Train’s Bulletin is a free monthly digital newsletter with contest announcements and original micro-essays on writing and craft; instructors can assign or discuss specific essays (examples cited: 'On Writing, Not Writing, and the Writing Life', 'On Revision') and search the Bulletin archives for teaching material. Encourage subscription and use of archive essays as concise pedagogical texts.
